deep.reconstruction:
Context: Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, Ch. 10. Euler states his conjectural rules for quadratic residues (his form of quadratic reciprocity, §§344-350) and asks what would follow from them and what would still need proof. Throughout, p is an odd prime, i is odd, and 'k is a residue' means x^2 ≡ k (mod p) is solvable with p ∤ k.

(End of §352) Conjecture for p = 4nq − i^2, i = 2m+1: n is a residue and −n a non-residue. By the symmetry n↔q, q is a residue and −q a non-residue. Proved part: i^2 is a residue and 4nq ≡ i^2 (mod p). So 4nq is a residue, and since 4 is a square, nq ≡ (i/2)^2 is a residue.

§353. Granting the conjectures, let p = 4nq + i^2 be prime. Then n and −n are residues, hence so are na^2 and −na^2. So there are x, y with p | x^2 − na^2 and p | y^2 + na^2.

§354. For p = 4nq − i^2 prime, na^2 is a residue, so x^2 ≡ na^2 is solvable. Since −na^2 is a non-residue, p never divides y^2 + na^2.

§355 (a genuine reduction). Since p = 4nq + i^2 ≡ 1 (mod 4), −1 is a residue. So for any f there is g with p | f^2 + g^2. If p | x^2 − na^2, choose y with p | x^2 + y^2. Then y^2 + na^2 = (x^2 + y^2) − (x^2 − na^2) ≡ 0. Thus for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), '+n residue' implies '−n residue'.

§356. For p = 4nq − i^2 ≡ 3 (mod 4), p divides no sum x^2 + y^2 with p ∤ xy (implicit). If p | x^2 − na^2 and p | y^2 + na^2, then p | x^2 + y^2, which is absurd. Hence −na^2 is a non-residue once na^2 is a residue.

§357. Let d = 4nq + i^2. From d | x^2 + na^2 and, by n↔q symmetry, d | y^2 + qa^2, we get d | qx^2 − ny^2. The identity is qx^2 − ny^2 = q(x^2 + na^2) − n(y^2 + qa^2). Likewise from d | y^2 − qa^2 we get d | qx^2 + ny^2, via qx^2 + ny^2 = q(x^2 + na^2) + n(y^2 − qa^2).

§358. Let d = 4nq − i^2. From d | x^2 − na^2 and d | y^2 − qa^2 we get d | qx^2 − ny^2 = q(x^2 − na^2) − n(y^2 − qa^2). Suppose d | qx^2 + ny^2 with x chosen so that x^2 ≡ na^2 (granted). Then ny^2 ≡ −nqa^2, so y^2 ≡ −qa^2, contradicting '−q non-residue'. Hence no qx^2 + ny^2 is divisible by d.

§359-360. These propositions would not settle the other observations, e.g. §345. In modern terms §345 says: if b^2 − na^2 ≡ 0 (mod d), i.e. n is a square mod d, then for every prime p ≡ ±d (mod 4n), and more generally p ≡ ±d·i^2, there is x with p | x^2 − na^2. That is, (n/p) depends only on p mod 4n and is invariant under p → −p.

§361. If d | b^2 + nc^2 (−n a residue mod d), then every prime p = 4nq + d·i^2 divides some x^2 + na^2. In modern terms (−n/p) = (−n/d) for p ≡ d·i^2 (mod 4n).

§362. For primes p = 4nq − d·i^2 no x^2 + na^2 (primitive) is divisible by p. The Kronecker character for −4n is odd. Example: n = 3, d = 7 = 2^2 + 3·1^2. Euler asserts x^2 + 3a^2 has no divisors 12q − 7i^2 and lists:
- i = 1: 5, 17, 29, 41, 53, 65, 77, 89, 101 (≡ 5 mod 12);
- i = 3: 9, 21, 33, 45 (≡ 9 mod 12).
errors: §362 example: 21 = 12·7 − 7·3^2 is in Euler's list of excluded divisors, but 21 = 3^2 + 3·2^2 with gcd(3,2) = 1, so 21 does divide (equals) a primitive x^2 + 3a^2. Similarly 57 = 12·10 − 63 divides 42^2 + 3. The rule fails when gcd(i, n) > 1. It holds for the primes in the list (5, 17, 29, 41, 53, 89, 101, where (−3/p) = −1) and for 9, 33, 45, 65, 77.
§359: the printed text ends 'divisibile erit per 4nq + d' although the sentence (and §345) concerns 4nq ± d; probably a slip for ±.
§§356, 358, 362 tacitly assume the squares are not divisible by d (primitive representations, p ∤ xy, p ∤ na). Otherwise e.g. d | d^2 + d^2. Not a real error, but unstated.

§357 and §358 present d | qx^2 + ny^2 (d = 4nq + i^2) and d | qx^2 − ny^2 (d = 4nq − i^2) as consequences of the unproved conjectures. Both are trivially true: q·i^2 ± n·(2q)^2 = ±q·d. Euler notices the analogue on the next page (footnote to §368) but not here.
§360: '4nq ± d·i^2 prime' implicitly needs gcd(i, n) = 1. Otherwise the number is divisible by a common factor and cannot be a prime greater than that factor.

results.what: For p = 4nq − i^2 prime, nq is a quadratic residue (since 4nq ≡ i^2 mod p)
Conjectural rules: for primes 4nq ± i^2, ±n are residues resp. +n residue and −n non-residue; reduction of the −n case to the +n case via (−1/p)
results.modern_name: Euler's formulation of the law of quadratic reciprocity plus the first supplement (−1/p) = (−1)^((p−1)/2)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjectured 1744-1783), proved by Gauss 1796/1801; first partial attempt by Legendre 1785

results.what: Combination of residues: qx^2 ∓ ny^2 divisibility derived from x^2 ± na^2 and y^2 ± qa^2
results.modern_name: multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol / composition of residue conditions

results.what: (n/p) depends only on p mod 4n and on ±p; (−n/p) depends on p mod 4n but changes sign under p → −p; extension to p ≡ ±d·i^2
results.modern_name: quadratic (Kronecker) character mod 4n: even for discriminant 4n, odd for −4n; equivalent to quadratic reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjecture, E164 1744, E552 1783), Gauss (proof), Jacobi/Kronecker (character formulation)

results.what: Example: primes ≡ 5 mod 12 never divide primitive x^2 + 3a^2
results.modern_name: (−3/p) = −1 for p ≡ 2 mod 3; divisors of x^2 + 3y^2

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known reformulation of quadratic reciprocity in terms of primes 4nq ± i^2, together with deductions from it. It is printed in the Opera Postuma (1849) and discussed by historians (Weil, Edwards, Lemmermeyer). Nothing goes beyond what is already attributed to Euler; the only novelty is a small slip in the example list (21).

checkable.asserts: qx^2+ny^2 is trivially divisible by 4nq+i^2 (x=i, y=2q), so §357's conclusion needs no conjecture
qx^2-ny^2 is trivially divisible by 4nq-i^2, cf. §358

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(-3 % p, p) == -1 for p in [5, 17, 29, 41, 53, 89, 101])
checkable.asserts: the primes in Euler's §362 list never divide primitive x^2+3a^2
21, listed by Euler as an excluded divisor of x^2+3a^2, is in fact represented primitively (counterexample)
57 = 12q-7*3^2 also divides a primitive x^2+3a^2, so the i=3 pattern fails

checkable.sympy: all(jacobi_symbol(3, p) == -1 for p in primerange(5, 2000) if p % 12 in (5, 7))
checkable.asserts: §345/§359 instance: (3/7)=-1 implies (3/p)=-1 for all primes p ≡ ±7 mod 12

checkable.sympy: all(jacobi_symbol(-3 % p, p) == 1 for p in primerange(5, 2000) if p % 12 == 7) and all(jacobi_symbol(-3 % p, p) == -1 for p in primerange(5, 2000) if p % 12 == 5)
checkable.asserts: §361/§362 instance with d=7: (-3/p) = (-3/7) = +1 for p ≡ 7 mod 12, and -1 for p ≡ -7 mod 12

checkable.sympy: all(jacobi_symbol(n % p, p) == 1 and jacobi_symbol((-n) % p, p) == 1 for n in range(1, 15) for q in range(1, 15) for i in [1, 3, 5, 7] for p in [4*n*q + i**2] if isprime(p) and gcd(i, n) == 1)
checkable.asserts: Euler's conjecture (§350/§353): for prime p = 4nq+i^2, both n and -n are residues

checkable.sympy: all(jacobi_symbol(n % p, p) == 1 and jacobi_symbol((-n) % p, p) == -1 for n in range(1, 15) for q in range(1, 15) for i in [1, 3, 5, 7] for p in [4*n*q - i**2] if p > 2 and isprime(p) and p % n != 0)
checkable.asserts: Euler's conjecture (§352/§354): for prime p = 4nq-i^2, n is a residue and -n a non-residue

transcription_corrections: No substantive misreadings found; the machine transcription matches the image.
§359 final 'per 4nq + d' is as printed (image shows '4nq -+- d'), though the sense requires 4nq ± d.
